correctness.rationale: For all integer k>=3, the paper-defined morphism yields the published block decomposition; the final two letters of W_j are exactly (t_k(j),j). A length-three factor can cross only one boundary apart from the explicitly handled early W_1|W_0|n chain. The proof lists every internal and terminal boundary triple and establishes the converse by constructing appearances at the asserted witness stages, followed by shifts. The independent direct-morphism and block-recursion checker passed 88 finite-language equalities and 4131 bounded triple membership comparisons; the proof supplies the unrestricted quantifiers.

evidence: The MathDB public proof establishes the occurrence-generating-function denominator from eventual recurrences for arbitrary B, with no classification of which three-letter B occur. The 2020 suffix lemma supplies t_k(j) but no exhaustive two-sided boundary analysis.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The new theorem identifies exactly which triples occur, not merely the possible denominators for their occurrence sequences. It requires checking both possible boundary positions and the exceptional one-letter block, then proving realization of all six families under shifts. These statements are not equivalent to, or special cases stated by, the posted rationality result.

value.rationale: The source specifically poses length-three language classification as the first natural unsolved instance of its general factor-language problem. The theorem gives an exact uniform all-k classification rather than a finite sample, an exact stage-filtered description for every iterate and a constant-case membership test. These answer a mathematically motivated structural gap, not a routine numerical recomputation.
